title: Senses Arcade
intro: Six rounds on ultrasonic, IR, line following and debouncing. Get them right first try to earn ⭐⭐⭐!

rounds.prompt: What does an ultrasonic sensor actually measure directly?
options: The round-trip time of a sound pulse
rounds.explain: Time is the only raw measurement — distance is calculated afterwards using the known speed of sound.

rounds.prompt: A wall is angled at 60° to the sensor. What happens when you ping it?
options: The echo deflects away and never returns — no reading
The sensor reads double the real distance
rounds.explain: Past roughly 45°, sound reflects off at an angle rather than straight back, the same way light bounces off a tilted mirror.

rounds.prompt: An IR sensor reads HIGH under a white surface and LOW under black. Why?
options: White reflects the emitted infrared light back strongly; black absorbs most of it
White surfaces generate their own infrared light
It's arbitrary and could be wired either way with no physical reason
rounds.explain: The reading reflects real physics: light surfaces bounce IR back to the detector, dark surfaces soak it up.

rounds.prompt: A line-following robot's left sensor sees the line, right sensor sees the floor. Which way should it turn to recentre?
rounds.explain: The line sitting under the left sensor means the robot has drifted right of it — turning right brings it back to centre.

rounds.prompt: Why does a single button press sometimes register as several presses?
options: The metal contacts physically bounce for a few milliseconds before settling
It's a software bug in every controller
rounds.explain: Mechanical contact bounce is a real physical effect present in every switch, not a controller fault.

rounds.prompt: What does debouncing actually do to fix bounce?
options: Waits a short window after the first change, then trusts the settled reading
Physically stops the contacts from touching more than once
rounds.explain: It's a timing fix in software — outlast the bounce, then read the level once it's stable.
